title: A Meta-analysis of Heart Rate Variability (HRV) and Psychopathology: An Investigation Guided by the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) Framework
description: While low resting heart rate variability (HRV) is associated with various forms of psychopathology, patterns of specificity and non-specificity in the apparent transdiagnostic nature of resting HRV have not been systematically investigated. Existing research is dominated by disorder-specific studies, limiting conclusions about whether HRV reductions reflect mechanisms unique to particular diagnoses or a broader transdiagnostic vulnerability. Using the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) framework, this Stage 2 Registered Report synthesized evidence from 430 studies and 732 effect sizes (N = 62,264) to quantify associations between resting HRV and psychopathology at multiple levels of specificity—from individual disorders to higher-order spectra and superspectra. Across the hierarchy, lower resting HRV emerged as a robust correlate of most domains of psychopathology. For example, at the disorder level, lower resting HRV was significantly associated with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism, generalized anxiety, panic disorder, borderline personality, posttraumatic stress disorder, and major depression, but not with obsessive-compulsive disorder, social anxiety, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Psychotic conditions showed the strongest associations across all levels of the hierarchy, but sensitivity analyses indicated that these associations are likely influenced by study design and sample characteristics. Together with consistent moderator effects showing stronger HRV–psychopathology associations in samples with higher symptom severity, we conclude that decrements in resting HRV represent a transdiagnostic marker of systemic dysregulation reflecting illness severity rather than disorder-specific autonomic signatures.

title: Empirically derived phenotypes can reduce diagnostic heterogeneity
description: Diagnostic heterogeneity is a longstanding challenge for the classification of mental illness because people who receive the same diagnosis can differ markedly in their symptom presentations as well as in the mechanisms underlying those symptoms. High heterogeneity undermines both the clinical utility of diagnostic labels and the scientific accuracy of research that treats disorders as coherent constructs. In this study, we examined heterogeneity across six internalizing disorders (specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, generalized anxiety disorder [GAD], major depressive disorder [MDD], and posttraumatic stress disorder [PTSD]) using three complementary approaches to quantifying heterogeneity: 1) descriptive heterogeneity (how many symptom profiles can theoretically satisfy the diagnostic criteria, and how many are observed in practice), 2) person-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels capture people with similar symptom presentations), and 3) construct-focused heterogeneity (whether diagnostic labels group symptoms with similar patterns of association with external validators). Analyses drew on subsamples from a large convenience sample with elevated psychopathology, predominantly from Australia and the USA (n = 14,762, mean [SD] age = 38.0 [18.0]; 55% women). Results showed that specific phobia was consistently the least heterogeneous; social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, and GAD had mixed results; and MDD and PTSD were highly heterogeneous across all metrics. Notably, empirically derived phenotypes nested within each disorder substantively reduced heterogeneity relative to the DSM diagnoses. The study provides both a systematic multi-method approach to characterising different types of diagnostic heterogeneity, and a practical path toward more precise and informative constructs that can be implemented by rescoring existing data.

title: Surpassing the Average Therapist: Performance of Commercial and Open-Source Large Language Models in Official Psychotherapist License Exams
description:
Background: Mental disorders are one of the leading causes of disease burden worldwide. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising avenue for improving mental healthcare. However, whether LLMs can match human therapists on key psychotherapeutic competencies in standardized assessments remains unclear. To inform this discussion, we applied the human psychotherapist qualification standard to LLMs and examined the performance of contemporary commercial and open-source LLMs against human performance in official state examinations.
Methods: In this pre-registered observational study, 14 widely used commercial (e.g., ChatGPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) and open-source (e.g., Llama-4-Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) LLMs were evaluated on three official psychotherapist state exams from Germany. Questions and official solutions were independently extracted from a secure training platform restricted to registered trainees. Models produced concise final answers via standardized prompts. Two blinded raters scored all responses against the official solutions. Performance was compared with pass thresholds and human cohort averages. Sensitivity analyses focused on domain-specific performance across 10 domains (i.e., psychological, medical, pharmacological, guideline, ICD, healthcare system and legal, behavioural therapy, psychodynamic therapy, and other therapies such as systemic).
Findings: All commercial models and 7 out of 11 open-source models exceeded the pass threshold on all exams. Five models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-o1-preview, Llama-4-Maverick, and DeepSeek-V3) surpassed the human cohort average across all exams, in some cases by more than one standard deviation. title: Dysphagia and Dysphonia in Parkinson’s Disease: Pathophysiological Mechanisms, Treatment Approaches, and Clinical Implications
description: Parkinson’s Disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons, leading to a wide range of symptoms that significantly impact patients’ quality of life. Among these, dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) and dysphonia (voice impairments) are particularly prevalent, affecting a majority of individuals with PD and contributing to serious health risks and social challenges. Dysphagia affects up to 80% of individuals with PD, posing risks such as aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, and dehydration. These clinical manifestations can lead to increased morbidity and mortality, making early detection and intervention essential. Current treatment approaches for dysphagia include compensatory strategies, such as posture adjustments, swallowing exercises, and dietary modifications, as well as pharmacological interventions. However, given the progressive nature of PD, individualized treatment plans are necessary to effectively manage symptoms and prevent life-threatening clinical manifestations. Similarly, dysphonia affects approximately 70-90% of PD patients and results in vocal impairments, including reduced volume, breathy or hoarse speech, and monotone voice, which hinder communication and contribute to social isolation. The loss of vocal strength and clarity can lead to frustration, withdrawal from conversations, and diminished overall well-being. The Lee Silverman Voice Treatment (LSVT) has emerged as one of the most effective therapeutic interventions for dysphonia, aiming to improve vocal loudness and clarity. While LSVT has shown promising results, research on dysphonia remains less extensive than dysphagia, indicating a need for further investigation into optimized treatment strategies. Given the profound impact of both dysphagia and dysphonia, a multidisciplinary approach integrating speech-language therapy, medical interventions, and tailored rehabilitation programs is crucial. title: Stability in Daily Well-Being in Romantic Relationships Versus Singlehood Among Young Adults
description: To prevent daily life stressors from spilling over onto general well-being, individuals often turn to support networks, such as romantic partners that help stabilize emotions, when their own emotion regulation resources are depleted. While satisfying romantic relationships have been associated with higher general well-being, the daily dynamics remain underexplored. Since increased volatility in well-being and accumulation of negative experiences may act as early warning signals of affective disorders, due to loss of resilience to adversity, we explore how stability in daily well-being differs as a function of relationship status. Using daily diary data over four months, we compared differences in day-to-day dynamics of well-being in two propensity-score matched samples of single (n = 85; k = 8,330 observations) and partnered individuals (n = 85; k = 8,362). We found that single individuals experience more negative affect and higher variability and instability in multiple well-being aspects compared to partnered individuals, but no differences in resilience in well-being could be observed. Based on statistical process control, both groups were equally resilient to accumulating negative experiences and were more vulnerable to such experiences when interpersonal emotional support was less available. We propose that the higher stability in well-being observed among partnered individuals is due to the unique emotional support partners can provide compared to other support networks. Simultaneously, partnered individuals face considerable vulnerability if they are overly reliant on their partner for emotional regulation. Therefore, both groups need to have alternative coping methods for dealing with adversity when their support networks are unavailable.

title: Wellbeing, Energy, and Work Functioning Among Autistic and ADHD Employees: A Mixed-Methods Longitudinal Study of the Hybrid Digital Support Tool Brain in Hand
description:
Abstract
Autistic and ADHD people experience persistent employment inequalities. This mixed-methods longitudinal study examined changes in wellbeing and work functioning among 278 employed autistic and/or ADHD adults (196 by 6-month follow-up) using the hybrid digital support tool Brain in Hand (BiH) over six months. Quantitative measures of wellbeing, productivity, perceived work-related energy, and coping were collected at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months, alongside qualitative free-text responses at 6 months. Significant improvements were observed across all quantitative outcomes over time. Improvements in wellbeing were associated with improvements in productivity; however, exploratory analyses suggested this relationship operated primarily through changes in perceived work-related energy. Reflexive thematic analysis identified five interrelated themes relating to experienced change, including increased self-awareness, proactive management of work demands, improved capacity to engage with work, and barriers related to workplace context and tool suitability. Participants described developing more sustainable patterns of work engagement through improved awareness, energy management, and workload regulation. Findings suggest that wellbeing and work functioning may be linked through proximal changes in day-to-day work capacity, particularly energy-related functioning. The study provides rare longitudinal evidence within an employed autistic and ADHD population and highlights the potential of hybrid digital support approaches within workplace contexts.

title: Theorising the arts as a health-promoting behaviour
description:
Arts engagement—defined as participation in or receptivity to creative practices (e.g. music, visual art, performance, storytelling, cultural activities)—is increasingly positioned within a health behaviour framework, though this remains under-theorised. This Review advances a conceptual argument for classifying arts engagement as a health-promoting behaviour, drawing on health behaviour theory, behavioural science, and public health. It situates this within the evolution of health behaviour models, from rational-choice frameworks (e.g. Health Belief Model) to biosocial, socio-ecological, dual-process, and complex systems approaches. Arts engagement is argued to meet ontological definitions of health-related and health-promoting behaviours (e.g. Behaviour Change Intervention Ontology), as it constitutes an individual behaviour capable of improving health outcomes, intentionally or incidentally.

Two critiques are addressed: (i) that framing arts engagement as a health behaviour risks instrumentalisation, and (ii) that it implies uniformly positive effects. The paper responds by conceptualising arts engagement along a continuum from informal, intrinsically motivated everyday practices to structured therapeutic interventions, analogous to other health-promoting behaviours (e.g. physical activity). It further examines mechanisms through which arts engagement functions as a health-promoting behaviour, drawing on experimental, quasi-experimental, and epidemiological evidence demonstrating associations and causal effects across psychological, cognitive, physiological, and social outcomes. Emphasis is placed on studies using advanced causal inference methods (e.g. propensity score matching, fixed effects, g-methods, instrumental variables) and longitudinal modelling (e.g. cross-lagged panel models) to disentangle independent and bidirectional relationships while accounting for confounding and selection bias.

title: Investigating the prospective associations of dietary risk factors with the risk of incident depression and anxiety in adulthood: Evidence from the UK Biobank
description:
Background: Mental disorders are leading contributors to disease burden worldwide. Nutritional psychiatry research supports an important role for diet in the prevention and management of mental disorders, but the relevance of specific dietary exposures requires further investigation. We examined associations of Global Burden of Disease-defined food groups and nutrients with subsequent depression and anxiety outcomes in UK Biobank participants, following the Global Burden of Disease Lifestyle And mental Disorders Taskforce protocol. 
Methods: We used data from the UK Biobank, a large biomedical cohort of more than 500,000 UK participants. Dietary intake was assessed using repeated 24-hour dietary recalls collected between 2011 and 2012 and classified according to Global Burden of Disease dietary exposure definitions. Depression and anxiety outcomes were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 and Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7 in the 2016 Mental Wellbeing Questionnaire, after excluding participants with pre-existing depression or anxiety from the respective models. Associations were estimated using complete-case log-binomial regression models with robust standard errors, adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, and lifestyle covariates. 
Results: Analyses included 46,503 participants in depression models and 48,656 participants in anxiety models. Overall, dietary intake was generally suboptimal, with many participants not meeting theoretical minimum risk exposure levels across several dietary factors. In fully adjusted models, higher intakes of wholegrains and fibre were associated with lower depression risk, whereas higher intakes of sugar-sweetened beverages and sodium were associated with higher depression risk. title: Schools’ Respect for Identity-Based Differences and Student Outcomes: Examining the Relationship among Students with Varying Numbers of Marginalized Identities
description: When schools value diversity, students with marginalized identities exhibit better academic and well-being outcomes. However, most work focuses on one identity dimension (e.g., race, sexuality) at a time. Using data from the California Healthy Kids Survey (N=205,064 6th–12th grade students in 751 schools), we examined how the number of marginalized identities a student held, schools’ respect for identity-based differences, and their interaction were related to multiple outcomes (e.g., belonging, grades, reported suicidality). Looking across multiple dimensions of marginalization (i.e., race, income, gender identity, sexual orientation, and language spoken at home), we found that 1) more marginalized identities predicted worse outcomes, 2) greater school respect for differences predicted better outcomes, and 3) this association was stronger among students with fewer marginalized identities for some outcomes but equally strong across all students for others. These results highlight the importance of respect for identity-based differences for all students.

title: A large-scale comparison of formally diagnosed vs. self-identified autistic and non-autistic adults
description:
Introduction: An increasing number of adults identify as autistic without having received a formal diagnosis. However, there is a lack of systematic research on how self-identified autistic adults compare to those with a formal autism diagnosis. We examined the characteristics of self-identified autistic adults and compared them to formally diagnosed autistic and non-autistic adults.
Methods: Data were retrieved from the Cambridge Autism Research Database (CARD). Participants were aged 16-80 years and included formally diagnosed autistic adults (n = 3275), self-identified autistic adults (n = 917), and non-autistic adults (n = 11,911). We compared demographic characteristics, autistic traits (Autism-Spectrum Quotient; AQ), systemising tendencies (Systemising Quotient-Revised; SQ-R), self-reported empathy (Empathy Quotient; EQ), performance-based cognitive empathy (Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test; RMET), and co-occurring mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions across these groups.
Results: Self-identified autistic adults were older, more often female, and more likely to be employed than formally diagnosed autistic adults. They had lower AQ and SQ-R scores than formally diagnosed autistic adults, but higher scores than non-autistic adults, with the reverse pattern observed for the EQ. RMET performance did not differ between self-identified and formally diagnosed autistic adults. Both groups reported comparably high rates of co-occurring mental health conditions relative to non-autistic adults. Neurodevelopmental conditions occurred most frequently in formally diagnosed autistic adults, followed by self-identified autistic adults and non-autistic adults.
Conclusion: Self-identified autistic adults show a profile broadly resembling, but not identical to, that of formally diagnosed autistic adults. This supports their inclusion as a meaningful group to further explore in autism research while highlighting important differences.

title: A systematic review of the effects of cognitive and perceptual factors on X-ray baggage screening performance
description: An X-ray baggage screener plays a critical role in aviation security. However, evidence about which cognitive and perceptual factors are important for effective threat detection during X-ray baggage screening tasks remains fragmented. This review aimed to (1) scope the existing literature examining cognitive and perceptual factors associated with X-ray baggage screening performance, and (2) systematically synthesise evidence linking these factors to X-ray baggage screening performance outcomes. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a preregistered protocol, searches of six databases (2000–2025) yielded 24 eligible studies (n = 11184 participants) including manipulation and observational designs. Cognitive and perceptual processes appear central to effective X-ray baggage screening, particularly under conditions of uncertainty, time pressure, and low target prevalence. Evidence broadly supports theoretical accounts such as Feature Integration, Schema, and Signal Detection Theory, suggesting that performance relies on attentional feature binding, experience-based knowledge structures, and the ability to discriminate signal from noise. Training and experience were consistently associated with improved detection, including generalisation to novel threats, indicating development of flexible perceptual schemas rather than simple memorisation. However, this relationship is not uniform, with some cognitive assessments (e.g. mental rotation, search speed) showing limited or no improvement with experience, highlighting a tension between learned and potentially stable traits. Furthermore, existing “talent identification” tools testing specific cognitive skills are undermined by circularity issues. Therefore, despite intuitive links between cognitive skills, human factors, and X-ray screening performance, the fragmented and heterogeneous evidence base currently limits definitive conclusions and practical application within the aviation security sector.

title: Minutes that matter: A microburst approach to adolescents’ resolution of affect in response to daily stressors
description: Adolescence is a period of heightened stress vulnerability, yet the microtemporal dynamics of affective stress responses remain poorly understood. Using an ecological momentary assessment design with four 15-minute microburst-assessments within the first post-stressor hour, we tracked negative (NA) and positive affect (PA) in 288 adolescents (ages 12–21) over 14 days. Piecewise multilevel growth curve models, compared across three affective reference points (i.e., baselines), revealed sharp reactivity followed by rapid initial stabilization succeeded by decelerated recovery. Stressor intensity amplified both NA and PA reactivity and decelerated later NA recovery. Interpersonal stressors elicited stronger NA reactivity, whereas social company buffered PA decline. Adolescents with elevated internalizing symptoms showed profoundly reduced PA levels - exceeding corresponding NA elevations - alongside initially faster but subsequently decelerated PA recovery. Greater stress exposure robustly dampened affective reactivity, with effects on recovery varying by baseline specification. Results underscore the importance of temporally aligning theoretical constructs with methodological decisions.

title: “I just feel like every day I’m missing out”:  Young people’s experiences of living with Long Covid
description: Background. Long Covid is a multi-system condition that profoundly disrupts people’s everyday lives. While research on adults’ experiences is growing, little is known about its impact on young people. This study sought to address this gap, gaining an in-depth account of the experiences of young people with Long Covid. Methods. We adopted a participatory qualitative design, combining expertise from young people with Long Covid, and adults with experience of Long Covid and academic research, as co-researchers throughout the study. We conducted individual semi-structured interviews with 13 young people, aged 13 – 20 years (M = 16.6, SD = 2.1) between August 2024 and May 2025. Interviews focused on phenomenological experiences, education, social life, healthcare experiences, perceived impact of Long Covid and future hopes. We analysed the data using reflexive thematic analysis within an essentialist framework. Results. We identified four themes: (1)“It’s kind of been relentless”, describing the sudden onset of debilitating symptoms, pervasive fatigue, and invalidation by healthcare professionals; (2)“It really kind of takes away your identity”, highlighting profound disruptions to education, hobbies and social relationships – and to young people’s emerging sense of self; (3)“The supports just aren’t there”, reflecting systemic failures in healthcare and education, alongside stigma and inequities; and (4)“The uncertainty is quite difficult to live with”, capturing the mental toll of the associated unpredictability and isolation. Conclusions. Our findings demonstrate that Long Covid exerts far-reaching effects on young people’s physical health, identity, education and mental wellbeing, compounded by systemic shortcomings and stigma. Addressing these challenges requires coordinated action across healthcare, education and policy domains, with inclusive, holistic supports co-designed with young people themselves.

title: Shape features of white matter tracts associated with post-surgical speech production outcomes
description: Impairments in speech production occur at a high rate after surgical resection of primary brain tumours. Due to their spatial heterogeneity, tumours can be problematic for voxel-wise lesion-symptom mapping. In addition, lesion maps of resection cavities may not capture displaced/deformed tracts, limiting the accuracy of white matter disconnection approaches based on population average atlas templates. Here we explore whether shape features extracted from individualised diffusion MRI tractography such as volume, curvature, surface area, irregularity, and span of six language-related white matter tracts are able to predict long-term speech production outcomes in survivors of left hemisphere primary brain tumours: The arcuate (AF), uncinate (UF), inferior longitudinal (ILF), inferior frontal occipital (IFOF), superior longitudinal (SLF) fasciculi, and frontal aslant tract (FAT). Best fit regression models selected via cross-validation and both univariate and multivariate lesion-symptom mapping analyses including clinical and demographic variables were used to compare the predictive capability of tract shape features, atlas disconnection estimates, and lesion location. Lesion-symptom mapping failed to reveal any significant relationships with speech production outcomes. A model comprising atlas-based disconnection estimates from the UF, SLF, and FAT was able to significantly predict long-term speech production outcomes (R2 = 0.14). However, a model comprising shape features of the FAT, ventral (III) component of the SLF, and IFOF explained considerably more variance (R2 = 0.37). Finally, we show that, in this dataset, shape features uniquely predict 26% variance that is not accounted for by disconnection estimates, demonstrating their relevance for predicting speech production outcomes in post-surgical patients.

title: Rethinking Talent in Vocabulary Learning:  A Developmental Perspective
description: Educational systems have traditionally conceptualized talent in foreign language (L2) learning as a stable attribute that can be identified early through performance-based assessments. Within the domain of vocabulary learning (VL), this assumption has reinforced the view that some learners possess an inherent aptitude for acquiring new words, while others do not. This perspective article challenges such trait-based interpretations and argues instead for a developmental account of VL capacity. Here, VL is understood not as the passive expression of innate ability, but as a dynamic developmental process shaped by interacting cognitive, linguistic, affective, and contextual influences. We synthesize evidence showing that key components underlying successful VL in childhood—phonological and working memory, semantic network organization, fast mapping, metalinguistic and cross-linguistic awareness, lexical inference, and motivation—are malleable and responsive to instruction. We also highlight the role of socioeconomic context in shaping early L2 exposure and vocabulary trajectories, arguing that differences in outcomes are often misinterpreted as evidence of fixed talent rather than unequal opportunity. Neurocognitive findings demonstrate that the brain systems supporting word learning remain highly plastic across development and are shaped by learning conditions. Multisensory and embodied instructional approaches, in particular, have been shown to reduce performance gaps and disproportionately benefit lower-performing learners. On this basis, the article calls for a shift in VL educational practice and policy away from early selection and toward broad talent development. Educational systems should focus on designing learning environments that convert potential into achievement, thereby advancing both excellence and equity in language education.

title: The Relationship Between Parenting Styles and Children’s Problem Behavior During the Transition to Preschool: The Moderating Role of Salivary Cortisol
description: The transition to preschool is a critical period for children’s behavioral adaptation, during which parenting styles may play an important role. Yet children may differ in their sensitivity to caregiving environments depending on their physiological stress regulation. This study examined whether salivary cortisol moderated the associations between parenting styles and internalizing and externalizing problems during the transition to preschool. Participants were 68 Chinese children aged 2.5 to 4 years. Caregivers reported parenting styles and children’s behavioral problems, and children’s diurnal cortisol levels were derived from multi-day saliva sampling. Results showed that cortisol moderated the associations of authoritarian and authoritative parenting, but not permissive parenting, with children’s problem behaviors. Authoritarian parenting was associated with more internalizing and externalizing problems among children with higher cortisol levels. Authoritative parenting was associated with fewer internalizing problems among children with high cortisol levels but more internalizing problems among those with low cortisol levels. Permissive parenting was consistently associated with more internalizing and externalizing problems regardless of cortisol levels. These findings suggest that biological sensitivity to context during the transition to preschool is both parenting style-specific and outcome-specific. They also highlight the need to move beyond uniform recommendations about “ideal parenting” and toward more individualized parenting support that considers children’s physiological stress regulation and regulatory needs.

title: Understanding Work–Family Enrichment Through a Cultural Lens: A Scoping Review
description: The aim of this scoping review is to synthesize the existing research about the relationship between work-family enrichment and cultural dimensions. Four databases were used to identify relevant articles. An additional strategy of Google Scholar to search for relevant studies was performed. In all, nine articles were identified. The scoping review suggests that only three cultural dimensions are being analyzed: gender traditionalism, humane orientation, and individualism/collectivism. Furthermore, the review confirms that culture has an impact on both work-family enrichment and/or how enrichment is related to other variables in a different cultural context. Theoretical explanations of the relationships are provided. Results are discussed, and ideas for future research are proposed.

title: The CARES taxonomy: Five psychological qualities of adulthood
description: Maturity has been traditionally inferred from the attainment of socio-demographic roles, such as having a professional career, being married, and rearing children. In today’s world, these traditional ‘adult’ roles are increasingly delayed or even entirely foregone. Here, we introduce the CARES taxonomy to describe adulthood as the rich, dynamic, and rewarding phase of life that it is, independent of work, marriage, and parenting. CARES proposes that five psychosocial qualities are at the core of adult maturity: Cognitive maturity, the confidence in one’s knowledge and abilities; sense of Aging, the realisation that one is aging and that life is finite; self-Reliance, the feeling of control in life; Eudaimonia, knowing oneself and living in alignment with one’s core values and beliefs; and Social convoy, the network of relationships and level of social support in life. These five qualities have conceptual and methodological foundations in the psychological literature, map the cognitive, affective, and behavioural roots of psychosocial maturity, and form the basis of adults’ mental health and well-being. We outline how the CARES taxonomy differs from existing models of adulthood and offers a promising starting point for exploring individual differences in adult maturity.

title: Neurocognitive mechanisms of individual differences in cognition: a behavioral performance and EEG dataset
description: The Mainz Network Study provides comprehensive behavioral and multimodal neural data from 215 healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years from the general population, supporting research on interindividual differences in cognitive ability. Across three sessions, participants completed the Berlin Intelligence Structure Test and Raven's Advanced Progressive Matrices (general and fluid intelligence), three binding tasks and three complex span tasks (working memory capacity), a cued task-switching paradigm (cognitive control), and three elementary cognitive tasks indexing processing speed (Posner letter matching, Sternberg memory scanning, two-choice reaction time). Electroencephalography (EEG) data and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data were collected. Here, we describe and publish the behavioral data (reaction times and accuracies) as well as EEG data recorded during cognitive control and processing speed tasks and during resting-state. Behavioral and EEG data are freely accessible via a RDC-ZPID repository. All data are BIDS-organized and shared raw.

title: Everyday Optimal Competence in Later Life: Conception and Empirical Investigation
description: Everyday Optimal Competence (EOC) refers to the high-level expertise that older adults develop through years of practice and informal learning in activities that bring meaning and structure to their daily lives. Across four studies involving over 900 adults (aged 53–90) recruited in Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom, we aimed to (a) investigate the perceived value of everyday optimal competence in later life, (b) develop the EOCS, and (c) establish its psychometric properties, including its factor structure, validity, and temporal stability. Study 1 used qualitative interviews, which confirmed that participants found the EOC concept to be a useful and personally relevant framework to describing their daily expertise. Study 2 focused on initial scale development, with exploratory factor analysis supporting a four-factor EOCS structure, and preliminary evidence of convergent validity. Through confirmatory factor analysis and measurement invariance, Study 3 confirmed the 4-factor structure of the scale and its gender and age scalar invariance. It also demonstrated convergent and discriminant validity with conceptually related constructs. Finally, Study 4 confirmed the scale’s temporal stability through six-month test–retest reliability. Overall, the findings support the EOCS as a robust, multidimensional instrument for assessing everyday optimal competence. EOCS provides a new tool to examine engagement in meaningful activities across later life.

title: Epistemic disadvantage in open science practices
description: Open science advocates aim to address epistemic injustice and global power asymmetries in research infrastructures yet underestimate structural vulnerabilities and risks embedded in data sharing practices. Drawing on an ethnographic study of the GCRF South–South Migration Inequality and Development Hub (MIDEQ), we argue that even well-intentioned systems, such as the MIDEQ hub, do not reach these vulnerabilities. To capture these overlooked harms, we employ the concept of epistemic disadvantage, a category coextensive with, but separate from epistemic injustice. Epistemic disadvantage includes ethically justified data withholding and misappropriation within consensual systems, which is not captured by existing notions of extractivism as those focus on the monetization of epistemic resources without regard for the loss incurred by the originating community. To better account for these harms, we draw on two recent epistemic attitudes: the Book of Truths (BoT), which sees scientific truths as emerging through peer review, and the Book of Conversations (BoC), which values data for the interactions and reflections it provokes. Even when epistemic values recognize knowledge as relational and situated, extractivist harms persist. We offer an ameliorated concept of extractivism to include subtler, systemic harms rooted in epistemic disadvantage.

title: Statistical Reasoning regarding Possible Adverse Outcomes of Vaccination
description: Reports of adverse events following vaccination can heighten concerns about vaccine safety. Across two experiments (N = 602 U.S residents), we examine how individuals evaluate evidence for a causal link between a vaccine and an adverse outcome, focusing on two key statistical considerations: the background incidence (or base rate) of the outcome in the absence of vaccination and the number of adverse outcomes assessed. Participants repeatedly judged the strength of evidence that a vaccine had caused an adverse outcome as information about a vaccine trial accumulated. Providing base rate information reduced perceived evidence strength and concerns about vaccine safety, particularly when the frequency of adverse outcomes aligned with population expectations, with these effects being more pronounced among more numerate individuals. Explicitly translating base rate information into expected case counts further reduced perceived risk, including among less numerate participants. Conversely, explaining how monitoring many outcomes increases the likelihood of false positives had little impact on participants’ judgments, regardless of their level of numeracy. Together, these findings show how individuals’ numerical abilities interact with the presentation of statistical information to shape vaccine-related judgments, highlighting both effective strategies for improving risk assessment and persistent challenges in communicating complex statistical principles.

Gender as a Moving Target: Making Up “Woman” and How the Looping Effect Can Help Advance Psychological Theories
description: This paper argues that Ian Hacking’s concept of the looping effect refers to an empirical phenomenon, the analysis of which offers valuable insights for advancing psychological theorizing. As psychological knowledge increasingly permeates public discourse, accounting for looping effects in psychological theory and practice is more pertinent than ever. Psychological research often treats concepts like gender as stable, monolithic variables, despite evidence that psychological theories actively influence experiences, feelings, and behaviors. Current theorizing on gender fails to capture the complex ways women interact with both traditional and feminist concepts of womanhood, particularly in highly psychologized societies. Analyses of psychologization’s influence on the looping effects of “woman” are illustrated through, and informed by, excerpts from interviews with women from 12 countries. This paper extends Hacking’s account by proposing that looping effects are dynamic, context-dependent phenomena affected by variables such as psychologization, and should be empirically studied to improve theorizing and interventions. The interviews suggest that updating psychological theories of gender, including those applied to affective disorders and workplace inequalities, to reflect the growing influence of feminist ideals and psychologization on women’s experiences, feelings, and behaviors may better achieve scientific aims of explanation, prediction, and intervention in the West. Theoretical frameworks and methodological recommendations for capturing the looping effect to improve psychological theorizing are presented. I show how feminist conceptions of scientific objectivity ground these proposed frameworks and recommendations. (226 words)

title: Testing within-person correlates of daily fearlessness about death in young adults
description: Fearlessness about death (FAD) reflects a reduced fear of dying that enables individuals to act on suicidal thoughts. Understanding how FAD changes in real time is critical because suicide risk can escalate within hours. However, little is known about processes that influence FAD within brief time periods. Painful and provocative events (PPEs), affective lability and impulsivity have each been linked to suicidal behavior and may shape momentary increases in FAD, but prior studies have been largely cross-sectional. To address this gap, we enrolled 148 young adults with past year suicidal thoughts and/or behaviors to complete ecological momentary assessments five times per day for 21 days. Using multi-level modeling, we tested the impact of daily fluctuations in affective states (happy, sad, anxious, angry, ashamed, and hopeless) and impulsivity on same-day FAD, with daily engagement in PPEs as a mediator. Results indicated that greater daily lability in impulsivity, anger, sadness and shame was associated with increased same-day FAD. Contrary to hypotheses, these effects were not mediated by PPE engagement. Short-term increases in FAD may arise from rapid shifts in emotions and impulsivity, rather than experiences such as PPEs. Capturing these dynamic, within-person changes can refine suicide theory and improve real-time suicide risk assessment.

title: Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers' novel word learning
description: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning. For example, 14-month-olds benefit from talker variability when learning minimal pairs, but struggle when learning distinct-sounding words. Talker variability is found to be particularly beneficial for learning to produce novel words. All of these previous studies have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used an active learning paradigm wherein preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, and talker variability choices interact with active learning to predict production, but not comprehension. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children can make choices are benefit their own learning, informing theories of both talker variability and active learning.

title: Why Some Gestures Work Better Than Others: Toward a Model of Gesture-Supported Vocabulary Learning
description:
Gesture has emerged as a powerful multimodal tool in vocabulary acquisition, with converging behavioral and neuroscientific evidence for its facilitative role in second language (L2) vocabulary learning. Yet in both instructional practice and experimental research, gestures are often treated as interchangeable, despite systematic differences in their form and implementation that may substantially shape learning outcomes. We examine the sources of such variability and argue that gesture design should be treated as a theoretically meaningful and methodologically important factor in L2 vocabulary instruction and research. 
Drawing on embodied cognition, cognitive psychology, educational neuroscience, and gesture studies, we synthesize seven mechanisms through which gestures may differentially support L2 vocabulary learning: iconicity, sensorimotor imagery, motional salience, emotional salience, gesture complexity fit, cultural familiarity, and enactment potential. We contend that variation along these dimensions may influence the multimodal lexical representations, their accessibility, and durability. 
Building on this framework, we introduce the Gesture Memory Support Model (GMSM), a preliminary model for rating gestures according to their predicted mnemonic support. The GMSM provides a principled basis for gesture quantification, enabling researchers to incorporate gesture-related variability more systematically into experimental design and statistical modelling, while helping educators to make more informed pedagogical choices.  By foregrounding gesture design as a critical determinant of learning outcomes, the GMSM aims to promote greater methodological rigor and theoretical precision in research on gesture supported vocabulary learning.

title: Voice-Familiarity Benefit in Infant Phoneme Perception: Acoustic versus Exemplar-based Familiarity
description: Starting in utero, infants perceive voice information and preferentially attend to the maternal voice. In adults, speaker familiarity facilitates word and phoneme perception. The current study investigated whether a similar voice-familiarity benefit supports phoneme perception in early infancy, and whether this benefit is driven by acoustic familiarity with speaker voice, prior exposure to phoneme exemplars, or their combination. We tested 72 German-learning 3-month-olds, who were familiarized at home with two speakers. In the lab, infants received 5 minutes of training on a difficult native vowel contrast (/ɛ/–/ɪ/) from either one of the familiarized speakers or an unfamiliar speaker. Discrimination was tested with the electrophysiological mismatch response using three talkers: (1) the phoneme training speaker (familiarized or unfamiliar, depending on group), (2) the familiarized non-training speaker, and (3) a novel speaker (i.e., an unfamiliarized non-training speaker). This design dissociated acoustic familiarity (at-home familiarization) from phoneme-exemplar exposure (training tokens). Preregistered contrasts provided evidence against discrimination differences across test speakers when training was delivered by the unfamiliar speaker; this training might promote speaker-independent generalization, as predicted by abstractionist accounts of speech perception. By contrast, exploratory analyses revealed a voice-familiarity benefit in the group trained by the familiar speaker; this training may drive infants to rely more strongly on speaker-specific cues. Thus, the voice-familiarity benefit only arose when acoustic familiarity and exemplar-based familiarity were combined, suggesting that neither form alone was sufficient. Together, these results are consistent with hybrid accounts of speech perception in which exemplar-like and abstract representations coexist.

title: The Musical Meaning Inventory: Development and Validation of a State-Based Measure of Musical Meanings
description: Musical meanings are central to emotional experiences and music appreciation, but they also tend to be difficult to describe and organise. Particularly for empirical research, there is a need for a structured measure that would identify the likely broad areas of musical meaning that people consider to impact their specific situation and context. We developed a state-based measure of Musical Meaning Inventory (MMI) based initially on a music appreciation framework that was operationalised and evaluated in earlier studies. Here we tested the initially hypothesised three factors of Musical Meanings (Self, Source, and Structure) in a series of exploratory factor analyses (EFA). In this experiment, 180 participants rated items representing the factors within the context-specific vignettes. The EFA revealed a five-factor solution, which was in turn verified with a second EFA round with a new set of participants (N = 59). The emerging structure and the highest-performing items from the EFA rounds were used in a new experiment applying CFA (N = 100). The CFA results confirmed the existence of five factors within the musical meanings (structure, memory, identity, object, and culture). The psychometric properties of the inventory were excellent (high reliability, good to excellent discriminant and convergent validity, achieving strict measurement invariance) with 15 items in total. The new tool is well suited to research contexts where the dimensions of musical meaning require efficient, multidimensional assessment.

title: The Picture Description Stimuli Set (PiCSS): Development and evaluation of a set of stimuli for the picture description task
description:
INTRODUCTION: The Cookie Theft Picture (CTP) description task remains a cornerstone in the assessment of structured speech to detect cognitive impairment in neurodegenerative disorders. Longitudinal testing of cognitive changes requires validated, parallel stimuli to mitigate practice effects, yet robust alternatives to the CTP remain lacking. We developed and evaluated the Picture Description Stimulus Set (PiCSS), a set of parallel stimuli to the CTP. 
METHODS: Stimuli were constructed using normed visual elements from the MultiPic database to ensure consistent naming agreement. In study 1, different presentation modes were evaluated in N=1378. Based on this study, the stimuli were improved and a scoring scheme for the evaluation of the pictures was devised. In study 2, the final stimuli were evaluated in N=175 participants, using an optimized presentation mode to establish the psychometric equivalence of the stimuli. Bradley-Blackwood test for equality of stimuli means and variances and Cronbach’s alpha were calculated. 
RESULTS: Eleven of the twelve developed stimuli demonstrated statistical equivalence to the CTP. The set achieved high internal consistency (α = 0.79). 
DISCUSSION: PiCSS provides a validated stimulus set for longitudinal assessments. These digital-first stimuli are optimised for remote monitoring in longitudinal clinical trials. Stimuli are made available at https://osf.io/42puw.

title: Exploring whether the Conscioussness mediate the relation between the Presentation of False Self on SNS and Narcissism
description:
Narcissism has been consistently linked to self-regulatory processes involving impression management
and self-enhancement. Therefore we explore the prediction of false self-presentation on social network sites
through narcissism, and also when basic personality traits of BIG Five model are included as a mediators in those
relationship.
The present study examined the relationship between narcissism, as measured by the narcissism subscale of the
Dark Triad Dirty Dozen (DDTD, Dinid et al., 2018), and the presentation of false self on social networks sites (POFS

title: Context-dependent acoustic dimensions underlying voice discrimination: Evidence from interpretable machine learning modeling of human perception
description: Voice perception is often conceptualized as occurring in a multidimensional acoustic space, though the stability of its defining dimensions across contexts remains unclear. This study examined how voice discrimination varies by speaker gender and linguistic level (word vs. sentence), using behavioral data from Mandarin-speaking listeners who judged whether paired speech tokens came from the same speaker. Interpretable machine learning classifiers, both linear and tree-based, were trained on acoustic differences to predict ground-truth and perceived-identity labels. Across both label types, models performed well when trained and tested on the same linguistic level but exhibited asymmetric declines in cross-level generalization: sentence-trained models over-classified word pairs as different-speaker, while word-trained models showed the opposite bias. Feature importance analyses revealed a shared acoustic scaffold (pitch, formant structure, harmonic shape, spectral balance), alongside gender- and level-specific adaptations. Tempo cues (especially for male voices) and variability-based cues of spectral balance (especially for female voices) became more prominent in sentence-level discrimination, likely reflecting prosodic modulation and contributing to the observed asymmetry in cross-level generalization. These findings extend prototype-based models by showing that cue weighting flexibly adapts to speaker gender and linguistic level. A methodological issue in computing within-speaker variability for harmonic spectral features was also addressed.

title: From the Lab to the Classroom: Bridging Psychophysics and Psychometrics to Improve Adaptive Dyslexia Screening
description: As children learn to read, two skills develop in parallel: the complexity of words they can decode and the speed at which the word recognition system operates. Reading assessments capture these processes using both timed and untimed tasks, yet it remains unclear whether word processing speed and word complexity reflect separable dimensions of reading ability or two manifestations of the same underlying skill. Here, we independently manipulated word complexity and presentation time in a lexical decision task to test whether they constitute distinct axes of reading development. Through a research–practice partnership, we collected large-scale developmental data from 3,194 students spanning Grades 1–12 in the United States (English) and Brazil (Portuguese). Results showed that items presented with infinite presentation time were systematically less difficult but required longer response times than items presented under fast conditions for students with and without dyslexia across development. Importantly, word processing speed and word difficulty were well characterized by a unidimensional framework, suggesting that the increasing speed and complexity observed during reading development reflect a common underlying skill. We then leveraged these findings to design and validate a novel multi-stage adaptive-timing approach for dyslexia screening (N=14,393 calibration sample; N=841 validation sample). Results from a K–2 validation study showed that this approach improved screening precision and efficiency for beginning readers. By integrating the experimental precision of Psychophysics with scalable measurement frameworks in Psychometrics, this work illustrates how insights from basic science can be translated into universal school-based screening practices for early dyslexia identification.

title: A Megastudy of Behavioral Interventions to Increase Voter Registration Ahead of the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
description: In the United States, in nearly all cases, one must register in order to vote—yet, a substantial portion of the eligible electorate remains unregistered. Despite this, relatively little is known about how to increase the likelihood that a voter registers. Here, we tested the impact of 10 expert-crowdsourced, theoretically-based psychological interventions on a sample of eligible, yet unregistered, U.S. voters ahead of the 2024 presidential election (N = 12,896). Eight of the interventions increased intentions to vote, and five led individuals to click on the voter registration website. Escalating Commitment, which sequentially employed several social pressure strategies, was the strongest intervention across these outcomes. However, none of the interventions had a significant effect on actual voter registration or voter turnout. The results highlight a substantial disconnect between voters’ intentions and their ultimate behaviors. We discuss potential structural and psychological barriers that undermine the translation of intent into action.

title: Which coping strategies reduce negative climate emotions when participants get to choose their preferred strategy? A quasi-experimental investigation of meaning- emotion- and problem-focused coping
description: Coping with negative climate emotions is increasingly studied, yet much of the evidence is cross-sectional. Moreover, existing experimental paradigms typically assign participants to a regulation strategy, whereas in everyday life people choose how they want to cope. In this preregistered online study (N=320), we induced negative climate emotions with a short film clip and then allowed participants to choose one of three coping strategies: emotion-focused coping (EFC; acceptance-based audio guidance), meaning-focused coping (MFC; meaning/hope-based audio guidance), or problem-focused coping (PFC) operationalized as a consequential pro-environmental behavior task. Negative affect was assessed at baseline, post-induction, and post-coping, and trait climate distress and climate impairment were measured to capture individual differences. Preregistered analyses tested whether negative affect decreased after coping, whether changes differed by coping choice, and whether individual and collective environmental efficacy predicted selection of PFC. Results showed that EFC, MFC, and PFC were each associated with reduced negative affect from post-induction to post-coping, while between-strategy differences were small. Environmental efficacy was not a reliable predictor of selecting PFC in preregistered models. In exploratory models, climate distress was associated with stronger reductions in negative affect after coping and climate impairment predicted greater odds of choosing EFC or MFC over PFC.

title: Modelling Implicit Bias in Gender–Career Associations: A systematic comparison of language models
description: Biases in language and their reflection in language models have attracted researchers' attention, particularly with the growth of large language models (LLMs). However, many questions on the links between language models and people’s biased attitudes remain unanswered. In the current preregistered study, we focus on gender–career bias to examine the extent to which language models can be used to model behavioural responses in the Gender–Career Implicit Association Test (IAT).  We provide a systematic evaluation of a range of language models, including n-gram, count vector, predict (word2vec), and Large Language Models (LLMs), to determine how well they capture people’s behaviour in the IAT.  We compared response time data from over 800,000 participants from the UK and US against 25 language models, with a total of 675 model variants. We find that many language models, including large language models (LLMs), correlated well with human behavior. While results support previous findings for both predict and count model families, we observed that performance of LLMs was consistently different from that of simpler predict models, frequently exhibiting correlations in the opposite direction. Thus, our findings reinforce the idea that societal biases are generally encoded in language, but that large language models can exhibit behaviors different to classical language models. Study preregistration, code, and materials are all available from the project website.

title: Attentional Advantage in Gifted Children Is Selective to High-Demand Exploitative Tasks: Evidence from TEPR
description: The cognitive advantages of gifted children have long attracted attention, yet most evidence has been derived from behavioral outcomes such as accuracy and reaction time, offering limited insight into the underlying cognitive processes. This study adopted a process-oriented approach to examine whether and how gifted children differ from their non-gifted peers in terms of attentional resource allocation in exploitative versus exploratory tasks with different levels of difficulty. Fifty gifted (138.22±6.23 months) and fifty-one non-gifted (107.94±5.26 months) primary school children were recruited and completed an exploitative task and an exploratory task with low, medium, and high difficulties. Accuracy and reaction time were measured as behavioral level outcomes. Task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) was measured using eye-tracking and served as the physiological index of attentional allocation. Results showed that gifted children consistently outperformed non-gifted peers in accuracy across both tasks and all difficulty levels, with group differences increasing as task difficulty rose. The advantage of gifted children in reaction time was evident only at low difficulty level in both tasks. For TEPR, gifted children showed greater attentional resource allocation only in high-difficulty exploitative tasks, with no group differences in exploratory tasks. Taken together, these findings highlight both the stable behavioral-level advantages and the physiological-level selective resource investment strategies of gifted children under a variety of cognitive demands.

title: Extraordinary-high rank expectation as a cognitive predisposition forming religion
description:
White et al.’s (2024) comprehensive review of the Cognitive Science of Religion enriched the scholarly landscape by integrating perspectives from the cross-disciplinary literature rooted in three decades of scientific research. Having gained profound insights into the Cognitive Science of Religion through this academic endeavor, I try to contribute my perspectives, grounded in social cognition in children and infants, to extend the ideas articulated in White et al. (2024) concerning the cognitive foundations and motivations forming religious thought and behavior.
White et al. (2024) provide an overview of the “naturalness thesis” concerning the cognitive foundations of religious thought (Chapter 2.3). They introduced Barrett’s “born believers” view, based on empirical findings indicating that cross-culturally recurrent forms of religious thought and actions can be found in the early development of life, such as childhood. I try to supplement the “naturalness thesis” with another fundamental cognitive predisposition of religion that individuals develop from the early stages of life. Possibly from infancy, individuals possess the cognitive tendency to attribute high social rank to “extraordinary individuals” who are perceived as capable of achieving goals through means beyond the limits of ordinary humans or the physical world, namely an “extraordinary-high rank” expectation. I elucidate these ideas and present the related experimental evidence.

title: Attitudes Toward Open Science Practices Among German Psychologists
description: The wide adoption of Open Science (OS) practices is influencing psychological science positively by increasing openness, transparency, reproducibility, and replicability. Researchers are encouraged to openly share their data, materials, and reproducible code, and to pre-register their hypotheses, design, sample size, and analysis plans whenever possible. On the one hand, these OS practices incur objective and/or perceived benefits, thereby raising hopes among researchers. On the other hand, these practices may also incur objective and/or perceived costs, thereby potentially inducing worries, especially among early career researchers. To investigate researchers’ attitudes toward the application of OS practices in their research and teaching, we conducted a survey among members of the German Psychological Society (N = 596) in 2021. Across status groups, researchers agreed that psychological science generally profits from the application of OS practices and that OS practices will become commonplace in the future. Furthermore, researchers indicated increased trust in studies adopting OS practices. However, researchers of all status groups reported to mainly have experience with pre-registration but less or even no experience with other OS practices. Researchers, especially those early in their career, believed to profit from OS, but also reported worries of making errors, especially when it comes to openly sharing analysis scripts. We discuss the current state of OS implementation and propose interventions to facilitate the broader adoption of OS practices, thereby supporting the career progression of early career researchers.

title: Helpful but Not Trusted: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Ethical Concerns Among Health Service Psychologists
description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly available to psychologists, yet little is known
about how licensed health service psychologists are integrating these technologies into practice
or how they perceive their ethical implications. This descriptive survey examined AI use, ethical
perceptions, privacy and disclosure practices, barriers to adoption, and training needs among 518
members of the National Register of Health Service Psychologists. Roughly 57% reported using
AI for work purposes in the past six months; among AI users, 51.4% of AI users reported weekly
or daily use. The most common professional applications were answering work-related
questions, generating easy-to-understand explanations, creating presentation content, and writing
session or progress notes. Roughly 55% felt that AI is helpful in practice, whereas only 20.0%
agreed that they trust AI. Ethical concerns were application-specific, with the greatest concerns
involving AI-assisted test interpretation and report writing. Privacy and disclosure findings
suggested gaps between professional expectations and practice; 73.0% believed practitioners
should routinely disclose AI use to clients, yet reported disclosure was infrequent. Most AI users
reported that they had not entered protected health information into AI tools, although relatively
few reported using HIPAA-compliant vendors or business associate agreements. Among nonusers,
the most common barriers were ethical, privacy/confidentiality, and accuracy/reliability
concerns. Findings suggest that AI use in psychological practice is no longer hypothetical and
underscore the need for application-specific ethical guidance, privacy-compliance training, and
evidence-informed professional development.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, psychological practice, ethics, technology adoption,
health service psychologists
