title: Vitamin D intake during pregnancy is associated with attenuated Season-of-Birth effects on infants’ language.
description:
The time of birth within the year can influence life outcomes, a phenomenon known as a "season-of-birth effect". While this effect is well documented in relation to health, its impact on early development is poorly understood. We investigated this effect in the context of
infant language and cognitive development in Norway. In a first cross-sectional study, using parental reports of vocabulary development with 1187 infants, we found that 12-month-olds born in mid-April had lower expressive vocabulary than those born in mid-October. The second longitudinal study assessed 848 infants between 6 and 18 months of age using the Bayley Scales of Development and showed that infants born in mid-April had lower cognitive scores than those born in mid-October. Although both studies indicated lower scores for infants born in late winter, the second study also showed that regular prenatal vitamin D intake mitigated these effects, reducing season-of-birth effects for language development. These findings underscore the importance of adequate maternal vitamin D status to reduce seasonal disparities in early language development.

title: Identifying the visual and linguistic sources of reading efficiency:  A comparison of individual differences among deaf and hearing readers
description: Reading is a task that engages the vision-language interface, and the efficiency of this process may be related to how much of the text readers use to process visual and/or linguistic information during a fixation (i.e., their reading span size). Compared to typically hearing readers, deaf signers both read more efficiently (i.e., faster with equivalent comprehension) and have wider reading spans, suggesting a critical role for span size in reading efficiency. Using a linear regression analysis, we assessed the effects of two different span sizes (the word identification span, within which readers extract linguistic information, and the perceptual span, within which they extract the visuo-spatial layout), and reading comprehension ability, on reading rate for deaf signers (N = 50) and hearing non-signers (N = 109). For all readers, those with a larger word identification span read faster, but this relationship was weaker for the perceptual span, emphasizing the importance of parafoveal linguistic processing for reading speed. The effect of the word identification span was stronger for the deaf group, and only deaf signers showed a positive relationship between reading comprehension ability and reading rate (and word identification span size). These findings suggest that reading efficiency (exemplified by deaf signers) derives from an ability to extract linguistic information far from fixation in a way that supports both reading speed and comprehension.

title: The psychology of cringe
description: While cringe is an increasingly common term in social discourse and popular media—often used to describe a situation perceived as awkward or uncomfortable—we currently understand little about its underlying psychology and function in human social life. Across five studies (N = 1416; three preregistered), we examined the social cognition of cringe as a stable individual difference trait and as a fleeting affective state, investigating whether it is the same as, or functionally distinct from, vicarious embarrassment. We propose that cringe is a specific variety of vicarious embarrassment elicited by intentional, reputationally damaging social norm violations, that functions as a signal of normative competency—communicating recognition and alignment with group norms—and motivates norm compliance and enforcement. We first developed and validated the novel 20-item Cringe Scale to measure individual differences in trait cringe which we found positively predicted state cringe perceptions, incentivized donations, and behavioral intentions. Additionally, we found that cringe, as compared to vicarious embarrassment, was elicited more intensely by intentional and public norm violations, and was associated with heightened moral wrongness and punishment judgements as well as reduced empathy and prosocial motivation toward the transgressor. Path analyses revealed that perceptions of transgressor intent and norm violation severity mediated these differences. Together, our results establish cringe as a functionally distinct variety of vicarious embarrassment characterized by psychological distancing rather than empathic concern. The findings inform our understanding of an increasingly important self-conscious emotion and illuminate the adaptive social functions of cringe in social cognition.

title: Does the Speaker Matter: EEG Evidence on the Influence of  Voice Information on Phoneme Learning in Infancy
description: Infants acquire the sound categories of their native language within the first year of life, despite the lack of invariant acoustic features that define these categories across speakers and contexts. Given infants’ ability to process voice information and their preference for the familiar maternal voice, we investigated whether voice familiarity supports the acquisition of phonemes. Specifically, we tested whether infants learn a difficult native vowel contrast better from a familiar speaker compared to an unfamiliar speaker. During a 5-minute phoneme training, 71 3-month-old German-learning infants were exposed to a difficult native vowel contrast (/ɪ/–/ɛ/), spoken either by a previously familiarized speaker or by an unfamiliar speaker. In the subsequent test phase, measuring the electrophysiological mismatch response, we assessed infants’ ability to differentiate the vowels when spoken by either the training speaker or a novel speaker. Using Bayesian analysis, we found evidence against improved vowel discrimination after training with a familiar speaker. Instead, it was training with an unfamiliar speaker that resulted in facilitated vowel discrimination for a novel speaker at test. Our findings suggest that infants may not necessarily benefit from a familiar speaker during phoneme learning, particularly when the speaker is not a caregiver and thus lacks an emotional connection. Learning from an unfamiliar speaker, however, may enhance generalization across speakers, potentially due to increased attention driven by novelty.

title: Computational determinants of context-dependent preferences in probabilistic tasks.
description: A robust feature of human (and other animals) reinforcement learning is the influence of contextual factors on individual preferences. The behavioral hallmark of this effect is that when tested outside their original setting, options that were "best among bad alternatives" are often preferred over those that were "worst among good alternatives", regardless of their true objective value. Several computational processes have been proposed to explain the origin of such relative value encoding, most notably outcome normalization mechanisms such as reference-point dependence and range adaptation (primary relative encoding). However, it has also been suggested that context-dependent behavioral signatures may emerge spuriously from other computational processes, even when values are encoded in an absolute and unbiased manner (apparent relative encoding). Among these alternative accounts, choice perseveration and asymmetric update can be argued to play a role. To resolve this ambiguity, we employed a standard reinforcement learning protocol consisting of an initial learning phase, featuring rich and poor reward environments, followed by a transfer phase to assess cross-contextual preferences. Behavioral analyses of the transfer phase revealed robust signatures of context dependence across four independent datasets. We compared four distinct classes of computational models embodying primary relative encoding and apparent relative-value processes. Model simulations established the necessity of a hybrid architecture combining a primary relative value encoding mechanism with asymmetric update in order to adequately capture human behavior. While we developed a novel range-adaptation framework suitable for probabilistic tasks, Bayesian model comparison robustly favored reference-point dependence as the mechanism best adapted to the present contingencies. Overall, this work demonstrates that multiple computational biases coexist in human reinforcement learning and that signatures

title: Construction and Validation of the Deliberate Ignorance Scale (DIS)
description: While humans are often considered to have a fundamental drive to pursue knowledge, they frequently choose to remain ignorant even when it is important and easy for them to know. Termed as Deliberate Ignorance (DI), this paradoxical decision differs from another avoidance behaviors like willful ignorance (WI) and information avoidance (IA), which are more defensive responses. This research constructed and validated the Deliberate Ignorance Scale (DIS) using a formative composite scoring method to capture this construct through an exploratory study in a health context (Study 1, N = 322) and a confirmatory study in a relationship context (Study 2, N = 162). Factor analyses established a robust three-factor structure: Perceived Importance of Knowing the Information (PIKI), Perceived Ease of Accessing the Information (PEAI), and Tendency to Ignore the Information (TII). Results also showed that the perceived importance of knowing remains unaffected by perceived threat. This independence signifies DI as a strategic decision, not a mere defensive response like IA. The DIS captures this structural paradox of Homo ignorans by positioning individual along a continuum from active information seeking to deliberate ignorance under conditions of acknowledged importance of knowing and accessibility.

title: Brain connectivity-driven digital twins of decision-making for personalized psychiatric intervention
description: Precision psychiatry requires digital twin models that link brain characteristics directly to decision-making. Here, we present NeuroPolicy, a hypernetwork-based framework that transforms resting-state functional connectivity (rsFCM) into participant-specific parameters of a recurrent neural network, thereby enabling individualized trial-by-trial decision-making dynamics to be generated directly from brain connectivity. In simulations, NeuroPolicy recovered ground-truth computational structure with strong correspondence to the latent representation (r = 0.88), while achieving high prediction accuracy (0.758–0.774). Applied to the NSPN cohort (n = 274), NeuroPolicy achieved approximately 0.72–0.73 accuracy in cross-timepoint and zero-shot inter-subject prediction from rsFCM-derived individualized models. Crucially, its differentiable mapping enabled in silico intervention optimization, improving optimal-action rates in 78.2% of individuals (mean improvement of 0.115, Cohen’s d = 0.99) and identifying personalized intervention directions involving prefrontal and frontoparietal connectivity. NeuroPolicy provides a framework for zero-shot behavioral prediction and biologically grounded intervention simulation in precision psychiatry.

title: Beyond Dissemination: From Critical Science Literacy to Citizen Neuroscience
description: Neuroscience increasingly informs education, mental health, and public policy, yet its real-world impact remains limited, with misunderstandings and neuromyths persisting. We argue that the societal impact of neuroscience communication depends less on the volume of information disseminated than on whether it cultivates critical science literacy; namely, the ability to evaluate how neuroscientific knowledge is generated, modeled, and constrained, and to understand the inferential steps linking data to conclusions and their limits of generalization. In the context of neuroscience, we refer to this as critical neuroscience literacy to emphasize the domain-specific challenges of interpreting brain-based evidence. The primary barrier is not insuEicient dissemination alone, but systematic misinterpretation of neuroscientific inference once findings leave the laboratory. We advance three claims: first, that public misunderstandings often reflect limited insight into scientific reasoning and practice rather than simple information deficits about scientific results; second, that citizen science and dialogical engagement function as mechanisms for practicing such reasoning rather than as outreach add-ons; and third, that neuroscientists share responsibility for shaping the interpretive conditions under which findings are translated, particularly in education, health, and policy. Importantly, this self-referentiality is not merely descriptive but can be causally consequential, as interpretations influence beliefs, expectations, and environments that in turn shape neural systems. We outline implications for training, incentives, and professional norms within the neuroscience community.

title: Restricted Environmental Stimulation and Psychopathology
description: The aim of the study was to assess the possible influence of the overall context of a modified version of Chamber REST (Darkness Therapy - „DT“) on the psychopathological induction. The research sample consisted of 37 clients of the Beskydy Rehabilitation Centre in Čeladná who willingly underwent a week of restricted environmental stimulation - DT (a version of Chamber REST), during 2012 – 2013. The age ranged between 25 and 84 (M = 45.86; SD = 13.16). The sample consisted of 17 women and 20 men. The participants were selected by purposive voluntary sampling. A week before the DT stay, each of the subjects filled in the Symptom Checklist 90 (SCL-90). Three weeks after they completed the procedure they received SCL-90 again. The data obtained were evaluated by the SPSS software. When comparing the values measured before and after the stay in the researched modification of Chamber REST (Dark Therapy) environment, we found a significant difference on all scales and on a total score, too.

title: Fixed in English, not (that) free in Slovak: A contrastive study of weight effects
description: Weight effects have been extensively studied in English but remain largely unexplored in Slavic languages, where research has primarily focused on information structure. This gap raises questions about cross-linguistic generalizations in constituent ordering on account of general cognitive constraints such as processing efficiency. We address this through a contrastive acceptability judgement experiment examining weight and phrase ordering preferences in English and Slovak. Using the method of Magnitude Estimation, which is concerned with proportional differences in acceptability, we collected ratings from 40 L1 speakers of each language on sentences varying in weight order (Light-Heavy vs. Heavy-Light) and phrase order (NP-PP vs. PP-NP). Gamma regression models revealed that both languages show sensitivity to constituent weight, but with crucial differences. English speakers demonstrated a strong preference for NP-PP ordering and heavy NP shift. Slovak speakers exhibited minimal sensitivity to differences and phrase order and weaker weight effects, suggesting a greater flexibility in constituent ordering in general. However, we also find that linguistic factors pale in comparison to the enormous between-subject differences, which account for the majority of the explained deviance in the data. Our findings are in line with cognitive predictions of weight effects on constituent ordering, while also revealing some striking differences between English and Slovak that warrant further cross-linguistic investigation beyond this specific language pair.

title: Within- and cross-task cued congruency effects: evidence that control adaptation strategies can transfer between stimuli and tasks
description: Research suggests that people can adjust cognitive control in anticipation of conflict on the basis of arbitrary cues signalling situations where responses linked to goal-relevant and goal-irrelevant stimulus dimensions conflict (i.e., congruency cues). However, findings are mixed and several questions remain. First, can control adaptation be implemented solely based on the expectation of conflict (or its absence)? Second, what is the nature of such proactive control adaptation? Specifically, does it involve the implementation of apposite adjustments of control processes tailored to the expected level of conflict, or does it instead reflect task-specific strategies, such as an attentional shift to the task-irrelevant dimension, or even just the general recruitment of additional attentional resources? Finally, can this control preparation transfer and affect performance in other conflict tasks? Across three experiments, we used a cued-congruency task-switching paradigm and found that people can benefit from congruency cues (Experiment 1, n=40), and that this proactive control generalizes from a flanker task to a similar flanker task involving different stimuli (Experiment 2, n=51) and even to a completely different (i.e., Simon) conflict task (Experiment 3, n=50). Overall, our findings are consistent with a domain-general view of proactive cognitive control.

title: Facial and body actions speak louder than context when inferring facial expressions of emotions in naturalistic images
description: Inferring others’ emotions is crucial for survival. Much work focused on facial expressions; others argue that rich body and contextual cues also shape emotion inferences from faces, often based on experimentally combined face images and contextual cues. However, people may use a different strategy to infer emotions in real-world contexts where rich cues naturally co-occur. Here, we had US representative participants (N = 475) view everyday images (N = 1,125) and infer the targets’ facial expressions of 8 emotions. We modeled how rich cues in the images quantified by computational algorithms and US representative participants (N = 1,093) predicted inferences of facial expressions of emotions. We found significant predictions by not only facial cues (e.g., action units, facial structure) but also body cues (e.g., posture, high-level actions) and contexts (e.g., environmental valence, gist). However, these predictions were based on different mechanisms: Facial and body actions carried unique information that was unexplainable by other co-occurring cues, whereas other cues primarily carried information that was shared. Given the differential mechanisms, we investigated whether integrating merely cues that carried unique information was sufficient for predicting human emotion inferences. We built artificial neural networks that allowed for process-level manipulations: by lesioning artificial neurons, we found that neurons that were crucial for human-like inferences integrated rich cues asymmetrically beyond facial and body actions. Together, these findings suggest that naturalistic inferences of facial expressions of emotions may be driven by facial and body actions that are contextualized by other co-occurring cues to support a coherent interpretation.

title: Assimilation to External Cues: Comparing the Reliability of Anchoring Effects, Advice Taking, and Hindsight Bias and Exploring its Determinants
description: People’s quantitative estimates, such as judgments about the height of a tower or the distance between two cities, can be influenced by external values, including random numbers in the environment or another person’s estimate. We reviewed three distinct but related phenomena in quantitative estimation: anchoring effects, advice taking, and hindsight bias. These effects are assimilative; that is, estimates are drawn toward the external value. They are also robust and they exhibit medium to large effect sizes. However, previous studies suggest that the reliability of their measurements differs considerably, ranging from low (anchoring) to high (advice taking). In this project, we compared the reliabilities of the three phenomena using open data (Study 1) and a new experiment employing a homogenized paradigm (Study 2). Homogenization involves controlling for differences in the informativeness of external values, computing assimilation scores, and using the same setting and knowledge domain. In Study 1, we found that, consistent with prior research, anchoring effects were largely unreliable, advice taking was reliably measured, and hindsight bias showed moderate reliability. This overall pattern was [reproduced] in [the simulation of] Study 2. We conclude that although methodological factors contribute to variability, they alone cannot explain differences in reliability.

title: Influence of partial speaker face occlusion during audiovisual speech perception in age-related hearing loss
description:
Objectives: Older adults with hearing loss appear to benefit more from seeing a talker’s face during speech-in-noise perception compared to their peers without hearing loss, which is presumed to reflect a visual compensation mechanism such as cross-modal neuroplasticity that offsets hearing deficits. How these visual benefits arise is unknown. We hypothesized that availability of facial features modulates the visual speech benefit in older adults with hearing loss, which would be driven by differential deployment of visual attention to facial features.

Design: Sixty-five adults aged 63–80 with typical hearing up to moderate hearing loss were recruited from the local community. Participants viewed audiovisual word stimuli and verbally reported the perceived word. Speech audio was presented in speech-shaped noise set to the 50% speech reception threshold. The task was done in four visual conditions: full face visible, eyes and upper face occluded, mouth and lower face occluded, and full face occluded. Eye-tracking was used to quantify dwell time on eye and mouth regions in all conditions except when the full face was occluded.

Results: Word perception was significantly higher when the full face or mouth were visible, compared to when the full face or mouth region were masked. Participants dwelled on the mouth most when the full face was visible, and on the mouth when eyes were masked, and on the eyes when the mouth was masked. Greater levels of high-frequency hearing loss were associated with worse word perception overall, but contrary to hypotheses, this did not depend on the availability of facial features. Calculation of a visual enhancement metric also did not correlate with level of hearing loss. No association was found between hearing loss and dwell time on facial features.

Conclusions: Results do not support that greater hearing loss in older adults is associated with enhanced audiovisual perception or altered visual attention to facial features.

title: Object and Setting Identification in Natural Auditory Scenes
description: We encounter situations each day that require our auditory system to quickly interpret our surroundings. Auditory scene perception involves complex processes that allow us to identify both the setting and the objects within a scene, which are essential for decision-making, and situational awareness. While there is substantial evidence for distinct cortical regions and pathways supporting visual scene and object recognition, far less is known about how the brain processes complex auditory scenes and objects. This study aimed to determine whether distinct mechanisms underlie auditory setting and object identification and whether these mechanisms interact to aid perception. Participants listened to 200 natural auditory scenes of varying durations (1, 2, and 4 sec) and identified the setting (e.g., café) as well as the objects (e.g., talking, espresso machine, music) within each scene. Overall, performance was highest on the object identification task, and there was a significant interaction between task and scene duration, with a greater benefit of longer durations for the object identification task. Different low- and mid-level acoustic features of the scenes predicted performance on the two tasks. These results suggest that the auditory system employs distinct (and potentially interactive) computations for setting and object identification, allowing for quick interpretation of complex, real-world auditory scenes. The interaction between task performance and scene duration further suggests object and setting identification may operate on different temporal scales; objects might require more time for accurate individuation, while settings may be recognized more efficiently through global properties of scenes, such as openness or naturalness.

title: You’ve got THIS! Demonstratives as a multimodal pathway to early word learning
description: Function words like `I' or `some' are highly frequent in children's linguistic input but are not learned early, so we ask: do they play any role in early word learning? Here we test a novel hypothesis that demonstratives, a class of function words like THIS and THAT in English, generate word learning opportunities for young children because they provide multimodal cues to joint attention on labeled objects. Combining head-mounted eye-tracking with machine-learning modeling of naturalistic interactions between parent and child (19 months), we show that demonstratives provide augmented inputs that scaffold word learning. Our results suggest that these function words orchestrate attentional dynamics in multimodal social interaction, expanding long-standing learning theories and showing that children can learn words from the full richness of everyday experience.

title: The Calm Before the Cancel Culture? Development of the “Pressure for a Perfect Conduct” scale
description: Social media platforms have facilitated various ways to connect, influence, and surveil each other. A novel related concept is the idea of Cancel Culture, which previous research posits might impact the behavior, emotions, and cognitions of the general public. The construct of Pressure for a Perfect Conduct (PPC) has been proposed as a conceptual representation of the pressure individuals may experience to conduct themselves perfectly under the threat of being canceled. However, there is currently a lack of quantitative research employing this construct, as well as no validated instruments to assess it. With this study, we aimed to build and validate the first instrument capable of accessing the construct of PPC. We conducted three separate data collections: a quantitative collection with which we performed Exploratory Factor Analysis (Study 1, N = 304); a qualitative collection where we discussed the existing items with experts in related fields (Study 2a, N = 3); and a second quantitative collection with which we performed Confirmatory Factor Analysis (Study 2b, N = 307). Additionally, we tested and validated a short version of our instrument. Our results indicate that the proposed instrument is reliable and valid, and can safely be used to assess the PPC model, but warrants further adjustments. The proposed instrument can help unlock future research on the topic by providing a validated measure, grounded on a novel framework, capable of broadly collecting quantitative insights into the impacts of Cancel Culture at an individual level.

title: Inteligencia Artificial y Aprendizaje: Una Agenda de Investigación desde la Ciencia Cognitiva
description:
La integración de la inteligencia artificial (IA) en la educación escolar plantea nuevas
oportunidades y desafíos. Cada vez es más común ver tutores inteligentes, asistentes de
estudio y plataformas adaptativas en las aulas. Sin embargo, este desarrollo está ocurriendo
mayormente al margen de nuestro más cualificado conocimiento sobre la cognición humana.
Por esto, es imperativo revisar el potencial impacto de la IA bajo la lente de cómo aprenden
las personas. Los numerosos estudios de la psicología educativa han identificado principios
fundamentales del aprendizaje humano, por ejemplo, la importancia de la carga cognitiva, la
metacognición y la personalización de la enseñanza, que deben guiar el desarrollo y adopción
de las tecnologías. Un uso acrítico de la IA podría sobrecargar la mente del estudiante o
fomentar hábitos superficiales. Por el contrario, un uso informado teóricamente podría
potenciar el aprendizaje y no solo la realización de tareas. Esta ponencia pretende examinar el
uso de la IA en el aprendizaje escolar con enfoque en tres aspectos clave: (1) su relación con
la carga cognitiva, (2) su impacto en la metacognición y (3) la personalización del entorno de
enseñanza mediada por IA. Además, pretende plantear una agenda de investigación desde
principios respaldados por la investigación sobre cómo ocurre el aprendizaje, a fin de
incorpora los hallazgos de la evidencia más robusta.

title: A Few Psychometric Properties of Work-Family Boundaries Strength Scale: Results from Three Studies in Lithuania
description: Valid and reliable research methods are needed to assess the work-home boundaries. Data from three cross-sectional studies were used to test the psychometric properties of the Lithuanian version of Hecht & Allen (2009) Work-Family Boundaries Strength scale (internal consistency, discriminant, convergent and structural validity). Results revealed that the Work-Family Boundaries Strength subscales had high internal consistency. Adequate convergent and discriminant validity was confirmed. Finally, structural validity was confirmed by exploratory graph analysis and confirmatory factor analysis, which revealed that the two-factor structure of the scale had the best fit. The results showed that the Work-Family Boundaries Strength scale is a reliable and valid tool for assessing work-family boundaries among Lithuanians.

title: Let's be friends! People work together even when there is no incentive to do so
description: One distinguishing feature of human social intelligence is our capacity to flexibly coordinate complex behaviors, such as when working together to prepare a meal. What cognitive or motivational processes make such joint action possible? Here, we investigate the role that a \emph{preference to enmesh behaviors} plays in human coordination using a novel two-player virtual baking paradigm. Participants could either independently bake bread by bringing their own water and flour, or jointly bake bread by bringing only water or only flour to share. Depending on the ingredient options available, trials in our experiment could correspond to either the classic Prisoner's Dilemma, in which acting jointly is disincentivized by the payoffs, or a "Friend's Dilemma", in which acting jointly is neither incentivized nor disincentivized (though it remains risky since one's partner might not share). Formal analysis of equilibria and dyadic learning dynamics indicate that people work together even when there is no incentive to do so. These results provide preliminary evidence that a motivation to enmesh behaviors with social partners supports successful coordination.

title: Cryptic Re-perception: A Cognitive Framework for Creative-Critical Thinking
description:
Abstract:
Contemporary models of thinking frequently distinguish between creativity, defined as the generation of novel ideas, and critical thinking, defined as the evaluation of those ideas. While this distinction has been influential across cognitive science and education, it leaves underexamined a fundamental component of reasoning: the process by which problems themselves are interpreted and represented. This paper introduces cryptic re-perception as a distinct cognitive operation grounded explicitly in the cognitive and neural mechanisms of cryptic crossword solving, a domain that requires solvers to deliberately inhibit misleading surface readings and construct latent, non-obvious interpretations from the same linguistic material. Drawing on Ohlsson’s Representational Change Theory, predictive processing accounts of cognition, dual-process theories, research on insight problem solving, and the emerging AI literature on cryptic crossword disambiguation, the paper argues that many failures in reasoning arise not from deficits in idea generation or evaluation, but from fixation on initial interpretations shaped by prior experience. Critically, the paper addresses a gap in prior frameworks: the expansion grid proposed to operationalise structured reinterpretation is distinguished from existing heuristic tools such as SCAMPER and de Bono’s Thinking Hats by its grounding in semantic network dynamics and its derivation from attested neural mechanisms of inhibitory control and associative expansion. The paper further integrates this model with contemporary neuroscience and identifies three falsifiable predictions that distinguish cryptic re-perception from these prior frameworks and discusses an empirical research programme needed to test them. title: Insights from climate psychology for misinformation research
description: Climate change and misinformation are interconnected global crises shaped by tensions between individual, collective, and vested interests. Drawing on climate psychology, we distil six insights for misinformation research to strengthen policy relevance, systems thinking, and resilience to attacks.

title: Tracking the mind’s eyes: Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Domain-General and Domain-Specific Visual Mental Imagery
description:
Visual mental imagery (VMI) enables the generation of perceptual-like experiences in the absence of sensory input. Previous work has identified a network supporting VMI that includes frontoparietal regions, domain-preferring areas in ventral temporal cortex (VTC), and a domain-general region in left fusiform gyrus, the Fusiform Imagery Node (FIN). However, it remains unclear (i) how activity unfolds over time across these regions, (ii) what representational content they encode, and (iii) how imagery dynamics relate to visual perception.
To address these preregistered questions, we combined fMRI and magnetoencephalography (MEG) using model-based representational similarity analysis. Twenty-six participants performed imagery and perception tasks across three domains (Colors, Faces, Maps). First, imagery-related representations emerged after ~0.5 s and peaked around 1 s, substantially later than perception (~0.4 s), with no clear sequential ordering between domain-general and domain-preferring regions. Second, representational analyses revealed both domain-general and domain-specific information, with commonality analysis showing that the domain-general ROI (FIN) was predominantly driven by domain-general structure, while domain-specific contributions were temporally dissociable. Third, imagery and perception showed distinct temporal dynamics: perception exhibited an earlier, stronger, and more homogeneous pattern, whereas imagery was more sustained and temporally extended.
Together, these findings indicate that VMI relies on distributed and interactive processes rather than a simple replay of perception. Domain-specific representations emerge relatively early, while domain-general processes, including the FIN, may contribute to sustaining and integrating imagery content over time.

title: Comparing machine learning and conventional P300-based methods for deception detection: a systematic review
description: Machine Learning (ML) has the potential to address highly complex problems. Deception detection is a problem for which no optimal indicator has yet been identified. However, EEG studies represent a promising approach for this task. Conventional ERP-based approaches to deception detection focus on the analysis of the P300 at a subset of electrodes, leaving much of the collected data unused. This raises the question whether ML approaches can better predict deception by building models inductively from large amounts of data. The present systematic review gives an overview of EEG studies (k=12) comparing deception detection rates between ML approaches and those based on conventional P300 analyses. Both, ML approaches and conventional P300 analyses reached accuracy rates around 80%. Although ML approaches achieved higher detection rates in most cases, the difference was small, and there was no evidence that one method systematically outperformed the other. Linear discriminant analysis and support vector machines were the most commonly used ML approaches and achieved among the highest detection rates. Neural networks were rarely used but yielded the highest detection rate. Wavelets were the most widely used preprocessing features. Studies using more electrodes did not systematically yield higher detection rates. However, in most studies, the data were highly preprocessed. It therefore remains an open question whether relevant features may be lost during preprocessing and whether the use of more electrodes would lead to higher detection rates when using data with less preprocessing.

title: Public positivity and private prudence: Differences in prescribed optimism for thoughts and appearances
description: Research on prescribed optimism has found that people generally believe others should be optimistic rather than realistic or pessimistic. We argue that previous studies on prescriptions have overlooked the social context, i.e., whether a future outlook is thought about privately or expressed publicly, with public contexts evoking self-presentation concerns that could increase the value of optimism. Four pre-registered experiments (total N = 1249) show that people think others should be more optimistic in public than in private. In Experiment 1 and 2, using hypothetical scenarios, participants prescribed more optimism for public appearances than for private thoughts in both within- and between-subjects comparisons. Experiment 3a and 3b investigated prescriptions for positive and negative events related to two current high-importance topics, climate change and AI. Again, results pointed towards more optimistic prescriptions for public expressions than for private thoughts, and additionally showed more optimistic prescriptions for a highly involved role (a CEO) than for less involved roles (scientist or average citizen). The findings suggest that people do not endorse biased thinking about the future as much as they endorse putting on a positive face. These social and reputational concerns may have implications for communication practices of leaders and officials, and could contribute to distorted, overoptimistic perceptions of the future among the public.

title: Can we distinguish briefly-presented natural scenes equated in summary statistics and semantic meaning?
description: Our visual experience feels rich, yet early studies suggested that what we can report about the experience is limited to 3~4 items at a glance. To reconcile this discrepancy, some studies argued that our momentary experience is a compressed summary of the visual inputs, which allows us to understand the general semantic meaning (gist) of the scene, creating an impression of richness despite lacking in details. Conversely, others proposed that our experience is perceptually rich and specific, but we have a limited ability to access and describe its details in words. To distinguish between these possibilities, we invented a novel psychophysics paradigm to examine whether participants can discriminate between images that are equated both on semantic gists and summary statistics. For each of 100 natural scenes, we synthesised an image with matched summary statistics. In Experiment 1 (N = 100, completed), we collected gist descriptions for each image, and evaluated whether each image pair is semantically-equivalent. Using these image pairs equated in both gists and summary statistics, in a series of registered Experiments, we will perform a perceptual discrimination task on online participants and in-lab participants with immersive displays. Overall, our experiments will investigate whether our experience contains perceptual details that cannot be described in words.

title: Automated Temporal Speech Markers of Childhood Stuttering
description: A major challenge in speech-language pathology has been accurately and reliably quantifying speech (dis)fluency, particularly the perceptible speech disruptions associated with childhood stuttering. We used a custom Automatic Temporal Analysis of Speech (ATAS) pipeline to detect and measure pause and vocal events during oral reading in 60 school-age children (6–13 years old) who do (CWS, n = 30) and do not stutter (CWNS, n = 30). ATAS metrics include speech rate, total pause time, pause count, mean pause duration, mean vocal duration, and variability in pause and vocal duration. Our results largely supported our hypothesis that CWS exhibit a slower and more fragmented speech flow during oral reading than CWNS. This pattern manifests as a slower speech rate, shorter mean vocal duration, longer total pause time, and more pause events. Many of these temporal metrics are also associated with traditional measures of stuttering frequency and severity. Furthermore, increasing age was associated with faster speech rate, fewer pauses, and reduced event duration variability, particularly in CWNS. Machine-learning analyses across multiple classifiers and feature configurations showed that ATAS-derived temporal features improved individual-level detection of childhood stuttering beyond demographic and chance baselines. The strongest performance was achieved by a random-forest classifier trained on age and ATAS metrics, yielding accuracies up to 92% across folds (mean ≈ 69%) under nested cross-validation. Together, these findings provide proof-of-concept support for rapid automated temporal measurement of speech production as an alternative and complementary tool for the quantification of overt speech disfluency in CWS.

title: Purpose and agency in evolutionary biology and psychology
description:
Abstract
For more than 100 years, the prevailing perspective on evolution has been gene centric.  It is a perspective from which random genetic mutations that happen to lead to naturally selected adaptive phenotypes are seen as the causes of evolution.  According to this “Modern Synthesis”, “selfish genes” are insulated from any influences of organisms or their environments, and function autonomously.  This article presents recent molecular and biological research that has led to an "Extended Evolutionary Synthesis” in which an organism’s development and purposive agency are the drivers of evolution. In addition to the influence of development on evolution, the focus moves to understanding how the relations between evolution and psychology change when evolutionary biologists describe humans, and all organisms, as purposive agents in evolutionary change. The Extended Synthesis has far-reaching implications for psychology, including the possible roles that psychological factors can play in shaping an evolutionary future. 
Keywords: evolution, purpose, agency

title: Replicating insight, insights from replication: Methodological reform in creativity research
description: Over the past 75 years, psychological science has investigated creativity using established methods. These robust approaches have examined how individuals generate novel thoughts. Such rigor has helped the field shift toward open science, which values robust and reproducible results over novelty alone. Open materials, data, code, preregistration, registered reports, and replication all foster advancement. In 2014, the American Psychological Association (APA) published a special issue that called for greater emphasis on replication in creativity research and promoted stronger initiatives. Despite these efforts, creativity research still lacks a strong culture of replication. This issue likely stems from the fact that creativity research spans many domains and methods. To address this problem, researchers and institutions should prioritize reporting and critically discussing unsuccessful replications in insight problem-solving experiments. Researchers must champion transparent replication and preregistration, and journals should commit to publishing well-conducted failed replications. These steps will drive scientific progress. Robust replication challenges existing paradigms and fosters creativity by confirming findings or revealing new directions.

title: A Multimethod Study of Speech Perception and Language Experience in Yucatec Maya–Spanish Bilinguals
description: This study examines speech perception, language use, and language ideology among university-educated Yucatec Maya–Spanish bilinguals in Yucatán, Mexico. Building on recent work, we conceptualize perception as gradient and shaped by linguistic experience. We adopt a multimethod approach integrating (a) Visual Analog Scaling (VAS) tasks assessing perception of tone (Maya), vowel duration (Maya), and voice onset time (VOT; Spanish); (b) egocentric social network measures of language use; and (c) qualitative analyses of language attitudes and identity. Results show systematic differences across continua: tone elicited more gradient responses, whereas duration and VOT showed more categorical patterns. Gradiency was significantly associated with language experience, including Maya dominance and the proportion of Maya-speaking interlocutors, while consistency remained stable. Qualitative findings indicate that participants view Maya as central to identity but navigate institutional pressures that privilege Spanish. These findings support a view of speech perception as shaped by socially structured linguistic experience.

title: No Evidence of Word Segmentation in Monodialectal or Bidialectal 9-Month-Old Norwegian Infants
description: One of the earliest challenges in language acquisition is segmenting words from continuous speech. One mechanism supporting this process is statistical learning – the ability to track distributional regularities in input (Saffran et al., 1996). Although this mechanism is well established in monolingual infants, its role under within-language variability (e.g., dialect exposure) remains unclear. Norwegian is particularly relevant in this context, as it lacks a standardized spoken form and consists of a continuum of regional dialects differing in phonology, prosody, and grammar. This study examined whether 9-month-old Norwegian infants segment speech using transitional probabilities and whether bidialectal exposure influences performance. In a conceptual replication of Saffran et al. (1996), 91 infants (55 monodialectal and 36 bidialectal) were familiarized with an artificial speech stream containing four trisyllabic words defined by transitional probabilities. Segmentation was indexed by differences in looking times to familiar versus novel items using eye-tracking. Bayesian analyses indicated moderate evidence for the null hypothesis in both monodialectal (BF = 0.20) and bidialectal (BF = 0.18) infants, as well as for the lack of group difference (BF = 0.25). These findings provide no evidence for transitional-probability-based word segmentation in Norwegian infants at 9 months, regardless of dialectal exposure, pointing to potential cross-linguistic differences in the onset of early statistical learning.
